sections.markdown:
## C — Safe and responsible driving part one: defensive driving, safety belts and child seats, communicating, avoiding collisions, leaving and rejoining the road, animals, headlight rules, night, fog, rain and wet roads
Knowledge domain: the defensive driving mindset, belt and child restraint rules, how to signal intent and dodge a collision, recovering from running off the road, oncoming drifters and animals, headlight and dimming distances, and driving at night, in fog and in rain; snow, ice, skids and traction devices continue in part C2.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Safe, responsible driving rests on staying aware of everything around you at all times and watching for situations that could turn dangerous. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
Defensive driving means adjusting for vehicle trouble, the road surface, bad weather, heavy traffic, poor lighting and your own physical, mental and emotional state. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
You must be able to see to the front, sides and rear, so never load or equip the vehicle in a way that blocks your view, and remember that window stickers or objects can cut into it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
A defensive driver keeps track of the surroundings and of possible escape routes at all times. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
Oregon requires safety belts for every driver and every passenger in all available seating positions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
Wear the belt with no slack in the lap or shoulder part, and never put the shoulder strap under your arm or behind your back. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A02
A child must ride in an approved child safety seat until reaching 8 years of age or a height of at least 4 feet 9 inches, and the adult lap and shoulder belt must fit the child correctly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A02
Infants must ride facing the rear until they are two years old. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A02
Collisions often happen because one driver fails to see another vehicle or a driver does something others do not expect. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A02
You tell other drivers what you plan to do by signaling before changing direction or lanes, showing brake lights, using headlights, using the horn as a reasonable warning and using hazard lights when needed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A02
The three ways to avoid a collision or soften its impact are stopping quickly, turning quickly and speeding up. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A02
Stopping quickly works when you have enough distance to stop, and your owner's manual explains how to use your vehicle's brakes properly. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
Most vehicles can turn away faster than they can stop, so if you cannot stop in time, steer away from the collision toward an escape route you spotted by scanning. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
Speeding up can be the best escape when a vehicle is about to strike you from behind or from the side and the road ahead is open enough to get clear. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A03
If your wheels leave the road, do not panic or brake hard; slow down until you can return to the road safely. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A03
After running off the road, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the vehicle going straight. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A03
Steer back onto the road with only as much front wheel turn as needed, because a sharp turn can carry you across the road into oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A03
If an oncoming vehicle drifts into your lane, move as far right as you can, slow down and warn the driver with your horn or lights. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A03
Never swerve into the opposing lane to dodge a drifting vehicle, since its driver may jerk back into that lane; heading for the shoulder or ditch is usually safer than a head-on crash. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A03
Watch for animal crossing signs and be ready to brake or slow down when passing an animal. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A03
If you hit and injure a domestic animal, stop, make a reasonable effort to check its injuries, and report it right away to the owner, or to local law enforcement if the owner cannot be found. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A03
Stop for a horseback rider or someone leading an animal who raises a hand, or when the animal is clearly frightened, unless stopping would cause a collision; a raised hand signals a frightened animal. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A03
Do not honk or make other loud, sudden noises near a horse or other animal on the road. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A04
Reduced visibility or a wet, snowy or icy road makes driving hazardous and calls for lower speeds and longer following distances. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A04
Headlights help others see you at any hour, and they must be on from sunset to sunrise. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A04
Headlights must also be on whenever conditions make it hard to see people or vehicles 1,000 feet ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A04
When using high beams you must dim them once an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A04
Dim your high beams when you are following another vehicle within 350 feet, since glare in its mirror can blind the driver. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A04
Whenever you are required to dim your headlights, auxiliary lights such as fog lights must also be off. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A04
Driving at night or in bad weather with only your parking lights on is illegal. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A04
A vehicle stopped or parked on a road or its shoulder in limited visibility must show its parking lights. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A05
At night you react later because you can see only as far as your headlights reach, so adjust how you drive. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A05
To cut glare from oncoming headlights, look a little to the right of them and follow the road edge or fog line. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A05
Check often that your headlights, taillights and turn signals work and that their lenses are clean. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A05
Take care passing at dawn or dusk, because an oncoming vehicle may have no headlights on and you may not see it in time. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F36 | anchor: A05
Stay alert at night for bicyclists and pedestrians, who are harder to see in the dark. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F37 | anchor: A05
In fog, dust, smoke or any low-visibility area, use low beam headlights, because high beams reflect back as glare and make it harder to see. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F38 | anchor: A05
As visibility drops, slow down, watch for slow or stopped vehicles and obstacles, and be ready to pull over; if you leave the road, pull as far right as you can and turn on your hazard lights. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F39 | anchor: A05
Rain cuts how far you can see and lengthens braking distance, so on wet roads brake earlier and more gently than usual. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F40 | anchor: A05
Even a summer shower can make roads slippery when the rain mixes with oil and dirt on the pavement. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F41 | anchor: A05
Turn on your headlights whenever your windshield wipers are running, skip cruise control on wet roads, and keep the windows free of moisture. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec09-F42 | anchor: A06
Hydroplaning is when tires skim or float on a wet surface and you can partly or fully lose the ability to steer and stop, so slow down when roads are wet. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec09-F43 | anchor: A06
If the brakes get wet after driving through water, drive slowly and press the brakes gently until they respond, doing this as soon as you can. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec09-F44 | anchor: A06
Do not drive through flooded areas, because high water can make you lose control or stall the engine. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec09-F45 | anchor: A06
Snow and ice hide the road ahead and lengthen braking distance, so drive slower, leave more space, clear snow, ice and fog off the windows, and leave cruise control off. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0086]

Misconceptions: braking hard after running off the road is the wrong reaction, you slow gently first; swerving left into the other lane to avoid a drifting car is never the escape; high beams make fog worse, not better; parking lights alone are not legal driving lights at night; a light summer shower is not harmless, since rain mixed with oil and dirt makes the road slippery; cruise control is out on wet or icy roads.
Mnemonics: stop, turn or speed up are the three collision escapes; right, slow, warn for an oncoming drifter; low beams in fog, wipers on means lights on; slow, straight, gentle steer to climb back onto the road.
Glossary: defensive driving means adjusting your driving for conditions and other road users so you always have an escape route; hydroplaning means tires skimming on water so steering and braking fail; auxiliary lights means extra lamps such as fog lights; fog line means the painted line at the right edge of the road; child safety seat means an approved restraint used until a child is big enough for the adult belt.
Dynamic facts: headlight hours follow sunset and sunrise, which shift through the year, and the studded tire season and chain requirements in part C2 are seasonal and posted on the state road information site.

corpus_stability.reason: The Oregon Driver Manual is a two-year edition (the front cover names a two-year span and the back cover carries a single form revision code); fees and office details are sent to the DMV website rather than printed, and nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year.
